title: VIII. A Treatise On Smerdyakov
paragraphs: “To begin with, where did this suspicion come from?” (Ippolit Kirillovitch began.) “The first person to cry out that Smerdyakov had committed the murder was the prisoner himself, at the moment of his arrest — and yet from that moment to this he hasn't produced a single fact to back up the charge, not the faintest hint of one. The charge is supported by only three people: the prisoner's two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. The elder of the two brothers voiced his suspicions only today, and while he was, without question, in the grip of brain fever. But we know that for the past two months he fully shared our conviction of his brother's guilt and made no attempt to argue against it. More on that later. The younger brother has admitted he hasn't the slightest fact to support his idea of Smerdyakov's guilt, and has been led to that conclusion purely by the prisoner's own words and the look on his face. Yes — that astonishing piece of testimony was offered twice today, by him. Madame Svyetlov was even more astonishing: ‘Whatever the prisoner tells you, you must believe — he's not a man who lies.’ That is the whole of the evidence against Smerdyakov produced by these three people, all of them deeply invested in the prisoner's fate. And yet the theory of Smerdyakov's guilt has been noised about, has been maintained, and is still being maintained. Is that credible? Is it even conceivable?”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch thought it necessary to describe Smerdyakov's character, “a man who cut short his own life in a fit of insanity.” He portrayed him as a man of weak intellect with a smattering of education, thrown off balance by philosophical ideas above his level and by certain modern notions of duty, which he picked up in practice from the reckless life of his master — who was perhaps also his father — Fyodor Pavlovitch; and, in theory, from various odd philosophical conversations with his master's elder son, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who readily indulged in this pastime, probably out of boredom, or perhaps to amuse himself at the valet's expense. “He spoke to me himself about his state of mind during his last few days at his father's house,” Ippolit Kirillovitch explained; “but others have testified to it too — the prisoner himself, his brother, and the servant Grigory — that is, everyone who knew him well.”

“What's more, Smerdyakov, whose health had been undermined by his epileptic attacks, had no more courage than a chicken. ‘He fell at my feet and kissed them,’ the prisoner himself has told us, before he realized how damaging that statement was to his own case. ‘He's an epileptic chicken,’ was how he characteristically described him. And the prisoner chose him as his confidant — we have his own word on it — and frightened him into finally agreeing to act as his spy. In that role he betrayed his master, revealing to the prisoner the existence of the envelope full of notes, and the signals that would let him into the house. How could he help telling him, really? ‘He would have killed me — I could see he would have killed me,’ Smerdyakov said at the inquiry, trembling and shaking even in front of us, though by then his tormentor had already been arrested and could do him no harm. ‘He suspected me every single moment. In fear and trembling I hurried to tell him every secret, just to calm him down, so he'd see I hadn't deceived him and would let me live.’ Those are his own words. I wrote them down, and I remember them. ‘When he started shouting at me, I would fall on my knees.’”

“He was, by nature, quite honest, and enjoyed his master's full confidence, ever since the time he returned some money his master had lost. So it can be assumed the poor fellow suffered real pangs of remorse at deceiving a master he loved as his benefactor. Severe epileptics, according to the most skilled doctors, are always prone to constant, morbid self-reproach. They agonize over their ‘wickedness,’ they're tormented by pangs of conscience, often entirely without cause; they exaggerate, and often invent, all sorts of faults and crimes. And here we have a man of exactly that type, who really had been driven into wrongdoing by terror and intimidation.”

“He also had a strong premonition that something terrible would come of the situation unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovitch was about to leave for Moscow, just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov begged him to stay, though he was too timid to say plainly what he feared. He limited himself to hints — hints that went unrecognized.”

“It has to be noted that he regarded Ivan Fyodorovitch as a kind of protector, whose presence in the house guaranteed that nothing bad would happen. Remember the line in Dmitri Karamazov's drunken letter: ‘I'll kill the old man, if only Ivan goes away.’ So Ivan Fyodorovitch's presence seemed, to everyone, a guarantee of peace and order in the house.”

“But he did go away, and within an hour of his young master's departure, Smerdyakov was struck by an epileptic fit. That's easy enough to understand. I should mention here that Smerdyakov, weighed down by a kind of terror and despair, had sensed over those last few days that one of the fits he'd suffered before, at moments of strain, might be coming on again. The exact day and hour of such an attack can't be predicted, of course, but every epileptic can sense beforehand that one is likely. So the doctors tell us. And so, the moment Ivan Fyodorovitch had driven out of the yard, Smerdyakov, weighed down by his lonely, unprotected position, went down to the cellar. As he went down the stairs he was wondering whether he'd have a fit, and what if it struck right then. And that very apprehension, that very wondering, brought on the spasm in his throat that always precedes such attacks, and he fell unconscious into the cellar. And in this perfectly natural occurrence, people try to detect a suspicion — a hint that he faked the attack on purpose. But if it was deliberate, the question arises at once: what was his motive? What was he counting on? What was he aiming for? I'll say nothing about the medicine — science, I'm told, can go astray; the doctors couldn't tell for certain whether it was faked or real. Maybe so. But answer me one question: what motive would he have had for such a fraud? Could he, if he'd been plotting the murder, have wanted to draw the whole household's attention by having a fit right beforehand?”

“You see, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the murder there were five people at Fyodor Pavlovitch's house — Fyodor Pavlovitch himself (though he obviously didn't kill himself); then his servant Grigory, who was very nearly killed himself; the third was Grigory's wife, Marfa Ignatyevna, though it would be simply shameful to imagine her murdering her master. That leaves two — the prisoner and Smerdyakov. But if we're to believe the prisoner's claim that he isn't the murderer, then it must have been Smerdyakov, since there's no other possibility, no one else to be found. That's what accounts for this cunning, astonishing accusation against the unfortunate feeble-minded man who took his own life yesterday. Had even a shadow of suspicion fallen on anyone else — had there been some sixth person — I'm convinced the prisoner would have been ashamed to accuse Smerdyakov, and would have accused that sixth person instead, because charging Smerdyakov with this murder is simply absurd.”

“Gentlemen, let's set psychology aside, set medicine aside, set even logic aside, and turn only to the facts, to see what they tell us. If Smerdyakov killed him, how did he do it — alone, or with the prisoner's help? Let's consider the first possibility — that he acted alone. If he killed him, he must have had a reason, some advantage for himself. But lacking even a shadow of the motive the prisoner had — hatred, jealousy, and so on — Smerdyakov could only have killed him for money, to get hold of the three thousand roubles he'd seen his master put in the envelope. And yet he tells another person — and a person with the strongest possible stake in it, namely the prisoner — everything about the money, the signals, where the envelope was kept, what was written on it, what it was tied with, and, above all, tells him the very signals that would let him into the house. Did he do this simply to give himself away? Or to invite someone else, someone eager to get that envelope for himself, to join in the plan? ‘Yes,’ I'll be told, ‘but he gave it away out of fear.’ But how do you explain this: a man capable of conceiving such a bold, savage act, and carrying it out, tells someone facts known to no one else on earth — facts that, had he only kept his mouth shut, no one would ever have guessed!”

“No — however much of a coward he might have been, if he'd been plotting such a crime, nothing would have made him tell a soul about the envelope and the signals, because that would have been as good as giving himself away beforehand. He'd have invented something, told some lie if forced to give an account, but he'd have kept quiet about that. Because on the other hand, if he'd said nothing about the money, and had simply committed the murder and stolen the money, no one on earth could have charged him with murder for robbery, since no one but him had ever seen the money, no one but him knew it even existed in the house. Even if he'd been accused of the murder, people could only have supposed he'd committed it for some other motive. But since no one had noticed any such motive in him beforehand, and everyone saw, on the contrary, that his master was fond of him and trusted him, he would, of course, have been the very last person suspected. People would first have suspected the man who had a motive — a man who had openly declared he had such motives, who made no secret of them — in other words, the murdered man's own son, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. If Smerdyakov had killed and robbed him, and the son had been accused of it, that, of course, would have suited Smerdyakov perfectly. And yet are we to believe that, while plotting the murder, he told that very son, Dmitri, about the money, the envelope, and the signals? Is that logical? Does that make any sense?”

“When the day of the murder Smerdyakov is supposed to have planned finally arrived, we find him falling down the stairs in a feigned fit — for what purpose? First, so that Grigory, who had meant to take his medicine, might put it off and stay on guard, seeing there was no one else to watch the house; and second, I suppose, so that his master, seeing there was no one to protect him, and in dread of a visit from his son, might redouble his caution and vigilance. And most of all, I suppose, so that he, Smerdyakov, disabled by the fit, might be carried from the kitchen, where he always slept apart from everyone else and could come and go as he pleased, into Grigory's room at the other end of the lodge, where he was always put whenever he had a fit, shut off by a screen three paces from their own bed. This had been the standing custom, established by his master and the kindhearted Marfa Ignatyevna, every time he had one of his fits. There, lying behind the screen, he most likely, to keep up the pretense, began groaning and kept them both awake all night — as Grigory and his wife testified. And all this, we're meant to believe, so that he could more conveniently get up and murder his master!”

“But I'll be told he faked the illness on purpose to avoid suspicion, and that he told the prisoner about the money and the signals precisely to tempt him into committing the murder — so that once the prisoner had killed him and made off with the money, most likely raising a commotion and waking the household, Smerdyakov got up — am I supposed to believe this? — and went in. For what? To murder his master a second time, and carry off money that had already been stolen? Gentlemen, are you laughing? I'm embarrassed to put forward such a theory, but incredible as it sounds, that's exactly what the prisoner alleges. He tells us that after he left the house, having knocked Grigory down and raised an alarm, Smerdyakov got up, went in, murdered his master, and stole the money! I won't even press the point that Smerdyakov could hardly have counted on any of this beforehand — could hardly have foreseen that the furious, exasperated son, despite knowing the signals, would simply come and peer respectfully through the window and then retreat, leaving Smerdyakov his prize. Gentlemen of the jury, I put this question to you in all seriousness: at what moment could Smerdyakov have committed his crime? Name that moment, or you cannot accuse him.”

“But perhaps, it will be said, the fit was real, and the sick man suddenly came to, heard a shout, and went outside. Well — and then what? He looked around and said to himself, ‘Why not go and kill the master’? And how would he even have known what had happened, since he'd been lying unconscious until that moment? There's a limit to these flights of fancy.”

“‘Quite so,’ some clever people will say to me, ‘but what if they acted together? What if they murdered him jointly and split the money — what then?’ A weighty question, indeed! And the facts backing it up are remarkable. One does the killing and takes all the risk, while his accomplice lies to one side faking a fit, apparently in order to arouse suspicion in everyone — alarm in his master, alarm in Grigory. I'd be curious to know what motive could have driven the two accomplices to hatch such a harebrained scheme.”

“But perhaps it wasn't a case of Smerdyakov actively taking part, but only of passive acquiescence; perhaps Smerdyakov was intimidated and agreed not to stop the murder, and, foreseeing he'd be blamed for letting his master be killed without screaming for help or putting up a fight, obtained permission from Dmitri Karamazov to stay out of the way by faking a fit — ‘murder him however you like, it's nothing to me.’ But since this attack of Smerdyakov's was bound to throw the household into confusion, Dmitri Karamazov could never have agreed to such a plan. I'll set that point aside, though. Suppose he did agree — it would still follow that Dmitri Karamazov is the murderer and the instigator, and Smerdyakov only a passive accomplice, and not even that, but someone who merely went along with it against his will, out of terror.”

“But what do we actually see? The instant he's arrested, the prisoner throws all the blame straight onto Smerdyakov — not accusing him of being his accomplice, but of being the murderer himself. ‘He did it alone,’ he says. ‘He killed him and robbed him. It was his doing.’ Strange sort of accomplices, to start accusing one another right away! And think of the risk for Karamazov. Having committed the murder while his accomplice lay in bed, he pins the blame on the invalid — who might well have resented it, and, to save himself, might well have told the truth. He might well have realized that the court would immediately weigh how far he was responsible, and so he might well have calculated that if he were punished, it would be far less severely than the real murderer. But in that case he would certainly have confessed — and yet he never did. Smerdyakov never once hinted that they'd acted together, even though the actual murderer kept accusing him, insisting he'd committed the crime alone.”

“What's more, at the inquiry Smerdyakov volunteered, on his own, the statement that it was he who had told the prisoner about the envelope of notes and the signals, and that but for him the prisoner would have known nothing about them. If he'd really been a guilty accomplice, would he have offered that statement so readily at the inquiry? On the contrary, he'd have tried to hide it, to twist the facts or play them down. But he did nothing of the kind — he neither twisted nor minimized them. Only an innocent man, with no fear of being charged with complicity, could have behaved as he did. And in a fit of melancholy brought on by his illness and this catastrophe, he hanged himself yesterday. He left behind a note, written in his peculiar language: ‘I destroy myself of my own will and inclination, so as to throw no blame on anyone.’ What would it have cost him to add, ‘I am the murderer, not Karamazov’? But he didn't add that. Did his conscience drive him to suicide, and not to confessing his guilt?”

“And what happened next? Notes for three thousand roubles were brought into court just now, and we were told they were the very ones that had lain in the envelope now sitting on the table before us, and that the witness had received them from Smerdyakov the day before. I won't dwell on that painful scene, though I'll make one or two remarks, choosing trivial ones that might not strike everyone at first glance, and so might get overlooked. First: Smerdyakov must have given back the money and hanged himself out of remorse yesterday. And only yesterday, according to Ivan Karamazov, did he confess his guilt to him. If that weren't so, why would Ivan Fyodorovitch have kept silent until now? So — if he confessed, why, I ask again, didn't he set down the whole truth in the last letter he left behind, knowing full well that the innocent prisoner would have to face this terrible ordeal the very next day?”

“Money alone proves nothing. A week ago, quite by chance, it came to the knowledge of myself and two other people in this courtroom that Ivan Fyodorovitch had sent two five-percent coupon bonds, five thousand each — ten thousand roubles in all — to the provincial capital to be cashed. I mention this only to point out that anyone might have money on hand, and that there's no way to prove these particular notes are the same ones that were in Fyodor Pavlovitch's envelope.”

“Ivan Karamazov, after receiving such an important communication from the real murderer yesterday, did nothing. Why didn't he report it at once? Why did he put it off until morning? I think I have the right to guess why. His health had been failing for a week: he had admitted to a doctor and to his closest friends that he was suffering hallucinations, seeing phantoms of the dead; he was on the brink of the very attack of brain fever that has laid him low today. In that state he suddenly heard of Smerdyakov's death, and at once thought: ‘The man is dead — I can put the blame on him and save my brother. I have money. I'll take a roll of notes and say Smerdyakov gave them to me before he died.’ You'll say that's dishonorable — it's dishonorable to slander even the dead, even to save a brother. True. But what if he slandered him unconsciously? What if, finally unhinged by the sudden news of the valet's death, he genuinely imagined it had happened that way? You saw the scene just now; you saw the state the witness was in. He was standing, he was speaking — but where was his mind?”

“Then came the document — the prisoner's letter, written two days before the crime, laying out a full program for the murder. So why, then, are we looking for any other program? The crime was carried out exactly according to this program, and by no one but the man who wrote it. Yes, gentlemen of the jury — it went off without a hitch! He didn't slink respectfully and timidly away from his father's window, even though he was firmly convinced the object of his affections was with him inside. No — that's absurd, unlikely! He went in, and he murdered him. Most likely he killed him in a rage, burning with resentment the instant he laid eyes on his hated rival. But having killed him — probably with a single blow of the brass pestle — and having made sure, after a careful search, that she wasn't there, he still didn't forget to slip his hand under the pillow and pull out the envelope, whose torn cover now lies on the table before us.”

“I bring up this fact so you'll notice something that strikes me as a very telling detail. Had he been an experienced murderer, and had he committed the murder purely for money, would he have left that torn envelope lying on the floor beside the corpse, right where it was found? Had it been Smerdyakov, say, murdering his master to rob him, he would simply have carried the envelope away with him, without bothering to tear it open over his victim's body, because he'd have known for certain the notes were inside — he'd watched them put in and the envelope sealed. And had he taken the envelope with him, no one would ever have known about the robbery at all. I ask you, gentlemen: would Smerdyakov have behaved that way? Would he have left the envelope on the floor?”

“No — this was the act of a frantic murderer, a murderer who wasn't a thief and had never stolen anything before that day, who snatched the notes from under the pillow not like a thief stealing them, but like a man seizing back his own property from the thief who'd stolen it. Because that was the idea that had become an almost insane obsession for Dmitri Karamazov regarding that money. And pouncing on the envelope, which he'd never laid eyes on before, he tore it open to make sure the money was really there, then ran off with it in his pocket, not even pausing to consider that he'd left behind a devastating piece of evidence against himself in that torn envelope on the floor. All because it was a Karamazov, not a Smerdyakov — he didn't think, didn't stop to reason, and how could he? He ran; he heard the servant cry out behind him; the old man caught up with him, seized him, and was felled to the ground by the brass pestle.”

“The prisoner, moved by pity, jumped down to look at him. Would you believe it — he tells us he jumped down out of pity, out of compassion, to see whether there was anything he could do for him. Was that really a moment for compassion? No — he jumped down simply to find out for certain whether the sole witness to his crime was dead or alive. Any other feeling, any other motive, would be unnatural. Notice that he troubled himself over Grigory, wiped his head with a handkerchief, and, once he'd convinced himself the old man was dead, ran to his mistress's lodgings, dazed and covered in blood. How is it he never once thought he was covered in blood and would be caught at once? But the prisoner himself insists he didn't even notice he was covered in blood. That can be believed — it's entirely possible; that's exactly what happens to criminals at such moments. On one point they'll display diabolical cunning, while another slips past them entirely. But at that moment he was thinking of one thing only — where was she? He wanted to find out at once where she was, so he ran to her lodgings, and there learned an unexpected, astonishing piece of news — she'd gone off to Mokroe to meet her first lover.”
